inline.s: Śāriputra, in a future age there will be monks who carefully observe the two hundred and fifty precepts, yet in whom thoughts of pride arise, and they will think: “I am the one who observes the precepts; the others do not.” Thus they look down upon others and are without reverence. They will think: “I am the one of wide learning; the others are not.” Śāriputra, at that time there will be many monks who value only the keeping of precepts, who practice the life of the forest hermitage, who well guard the body of precepts and act in accord with what they teach, who diligently recite the scriptures in seeking to penetrate the Buddha’s Dharma. Persons such as these give rise to the pride of wide learning and the pride of the forest life, and are given to anger; their minds are constantly defiled, deeply harboring a venomous heart of miserliness, greed, and hatred; they are dull and ignorant, and over trifling causes they stir up great affairs. These persons, their minds covered with anger, mutually accuse one another of faults, saying that the other has broken the precepts, broken the views, broken the life, and broken all dignity of deportment.

[Two hundred and fifty precepts]The full precepts of a bhikṣu. [Forest-hermitage practice]The bhikṣu dwells constantly in the forest hermitage and does not dwell among the laity; it is one of the twelve dhūta practices. [Araṇya]Translated into Chinese as “the place of stillness,” a general term for the monastic dwellings in which a bhikṣu resides. [Āraṇya]The same as araṇya.

[Śāriputra, within such an order of monks there will be good bhikṣus who, without bias or partisanship, stand in the middle; yet being amidst those evil ones they too are drawn into mutual criticism and wrangling that never ceases, and they cannot gain peace to sit in meditation or to read the scriptures; both the lay and the monastic are thus disturbed. Even so, Śāriputra, at that time there will be many monks — of one year, two years, three years, up to nine years of ordination — who treat the elders with contempt and are without respect. These persons, having left home and received the precepts, for the most part act contrary to the Dharma, and toward their teachers and preceptors they likewise show no reverence.]

Śāriputra, within such an order of monks there will be good bhikṣus who, though without bias or partisanship (taking no side), yet being placed among evil monks will also be drawn with them into mutual criticism and wrangling that never ceases, and they cannot gain peace to sit in meditation or to read the scriptures; both the lay and the monastic are disturbed. Even so, Śāriputra, at that time there will be many monks — those of one year, two years, three years, up to nine years of ordination — who treat the elders with contempt and are without respect. Though these persons have left home and received the precepts, for the most part they act contrary to the Dharma and toward their teachers and preceptors they likewise show no reverence.

[Ordination age]The number of years since a bhikṣu received the full precepts. [Elder]A rank within the monastic community, standing below the abbot, and above all others except the abbot; hence called “elder.” Here it refers to bhikṣus of high ordination age who occupy the upper seats.

[Śāriputra, at that time the young bhikṣus and those of old who left home but have no refuge will mutually despise one another. The disciples gathered by a bhikṣu of ten years’ ordination will all be without reverence, without dignity of deportment, and without the proper rules, nor will they act according to the Dharma. Śāriputra, at that time these evil persons, fully endowed with greed, hatred, and delusion, will mutually despise one another and be without respect; because they go against one another, my Dharma will be destroyed. Śāriputra, at that time these many deluded persons will commit the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, and having committed them they will fall into the evil realms.]

Śāriputra, at that time the young bhikṣus and those of old who left home but have no refuge will mutually despise one another. The disciples gathered by a bhikṣu of ten years’ ordination (according to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu may gather disciples only after ten years of ordination) will all be without reverence, without dignity of deportment, without the proper rules, nor will they act according to the Dharma. Śāriputra, at that time these evil persons, fully endowed with greed, hatred, and delusion, will mutually despise one another and be without respect; because they go against one another, the true Dharma will be destroyed. Śāriputra, at that time these many deluded persons will commit the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, and having committed them they will fall into the evil realms.

[Śāriputra, I now declare to you plainly: a good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should not, at that time, enter the assembly — not even for a single night — except for one who is an arhat whose defilements are already extinguished, or a sick bhikṣu who has a connection therein. Why? Śāriputra, at that time people’s poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion will be fierce, and the dread of not being able to live will constantly press upon them. The good man who seeks his own benefit should always dwell alone in the mountain forests and quiet places, even to the end of his life, dying like a wild beast.]

Śāriputra, I now tell you plainly: a good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should not, at that time, enter the assembly and dwell together with precept-breaking monks — not even for a single night — unless he is an arhat whose defilements are already extinguished, or a sick bhikṣu who needs care. Why? Śāriputra, at that time people’s poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion will be fierce, and the dread of not being able to live will constantly press upon them; they all pursue fame and profit. The good man who seeks his own benefit should always dwell alone in the mountain forests and quiet places, even to the end of his life dying like a wild beast, and never dwell together with evil persons.
[Dread of not being able to live]The fear that one may not be able to keep oneself alive, leading one to scheme after and hoard wealth.

[Śāriputra, I now declare to you plainly: this true Dharma of mine will not long abide in the world. Why? Because the merit and wholesome roots of sentient beings are exhausted, and the defiled age is near at hand. A good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should give rise to this thought of revulsion: “How shall I bear to see this Dharma being thrown into confusion, and to see this evil age of the śramaṇas, this difficult time?” I should strive with a diligent mind and attain the path and fruit quickly.]

Śāriputra, I now tell you plainly: the true Dharma of mine cannot long abide in the world. Why? Because the merit and wholesome roots of sentient beings are exhausted, and the defiled evil age is about to arrive. A good bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit should give rise to this thought of revulsion: “Why should I see this true Dharma thrown into confusion, and this evil age of the śramaṇas, this difficult time?” I should strive with a diligent mind and attain the path and fruit quickly.

[Śāriputra, in my Dharma there are no difficult matters — do not be anxious about clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. You should merely strive diligently along the Buddha way, and not value the wealth and offerings of the world. Śāriputra, listen well now, and I will tell you: if there is a bhikṣu who single-mindedly practices the way, a thousand crore of gods will all be of one mind and, with every kind of pleasing object, will wish to make offerings to him. Śāriputra, the offerings made by people to a bhikṣu who sits in meditation do not match those of the gods. Therefore, Śāriputra, do not be anxious that you will not be able to support yourselves. The true teaching of the Buddha is to be followed accordingly; do not use the emptiness of the ultimate truth to point out the faults of others. Why? Śāriputra, the great danger
(in ancient usage the same as “险,” peril)
is what is called gaining emptiness.]

Śāriputra, in studying my Dharma there are no difficult matters — do not be anxious about clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. You should merely strive diligently along the Buddha way, and not value the wealth and offerings of the world. Śāriputra, listen well now, and I solemnly tell you: if there is a bhikṣu who single-mindedly practices the way, a thousand crore of gods will all be of one mind and joyfully make offerings to him. Śāriputra, the offerings made by people to a bhikṣu who sits in meditation do not match those of the gods. Therefore, Śāriputra, do not be anxious that you will not be able to support yourselves. The true teaching of the Buddha is to be followed accordingly; do not use the emptiness of the ultimate truth to point out the faults of others. Why? Śāriputra, the great danger is what is called gaining emptiness.

[Do not use the emptiness of the ultimate truth to point out the faults of others]Do not, on the ground of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, point out the faults of others. If one, on the ground of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, points out the faults of others, then within emptiness one gives rise to a mind of possession and becomes attached to the marks of self and of others. If so, one cannot accomplish the supreme Buddha way; therefore it is called the great danger.

[Or there may be a bhikṣu who, having left home and received the precepts because of my Dharma, strives diligently within this Dharma. Even though the gods and men do not remember him, if he can single-mindedly and diligently practice the way, in the end he will not lack the clothing and food he needs. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s store of merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Śāriputra, after the Tathāgata’s passing, of the hundred thousand crore portions of the mark of the white hair, one portion is given to support the relics and the disciples. Śāriputra, were all the people of the world to leave home and follow the Dharma in practice, they would not exhaust one of the hundred thousand crore portions of the white-hair mark. Śāriputra, such is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit that the food and the things the bhikṣus obtain are all fully provided. Śāriputra, these bhikṣus should think in this way, and should not, for the sake of the things they need, engage in any of the wrong ways of living.]
